cues.text: Welcome back.
Today we begin current electricity by asking a very simple question: what does
it mean for charge to flow?
Current is the rate at which charge crosses a chosen cross section.
For a steady flow, current is charge divided by time.
More generally, I equals dQ by dt.
Imagine a wire cut by an invisible ring.
Every coulomb crossing that ring each second contributes one ampere.
In a metal, electrons already move rapidly in random directions, but those
random motions cancel on average.
An electric field adds a tiny organized drift.
That drift is slow, yet the electrical response of a circuit is established
through the field throughout the conductor.
Here is the microscopic connection.
If n is the number of free electrons per unit volume, each with charge
magnitude e, the cross sectional area is A, and the drift speed is v sub d,
then I equals n e A v sub d.
Notice the product: in one second, a slice of length v sub d moves through
area
A.
Its volume is A v sub d, so the number of carriers is n A v sub d.
Each contributes charge e.
One careful sign point: conventional current is defined in the direction
positive charge would move.
Electrons drift opposite to that direction.
Try this: if two times ten to the 18 electrons cross a section each second,
the
current magnitude is three point two tenths of an ampere, using e equal to one
point six times ten to the minus 19 coulomb.
That direction convention will matter in every graph and circuit we meet next.
The total current depends on how much wire we capture, so physicists also use
current density.
Current density J is current per cross sectional area.
For a uniform wire, J equals I over A, and the microscopic expression becomes
n e v sub d.
This is useful because it separates the local material response from the size
of the wire.
In a simple conductor, drift speed is proportional to the electric field: v
sub
d equals mobility times E.
Mobility, written mu, tells us how easily carriers respond to the field.
Combine those statements and J equals n e mu E.
The factor n e mu is called conductivity, sigma, so J equals sigma E.
Its reciprocal is resistivity, rho.
Let us use a quick application.
A wire carries two amperes through an area of one square millimeter.
Convert the area to one times ten to the minus six square meters.
The current density is therefore two times ten to the six amperes per square
meter.
It is not two amperes per millimeter in a vague sense; unit conversion is part
of the physics.
Now imagine the same current in a thinner wire.
The current may be unchanged in a series path, but J becomes larger because A
is smaller.
That larger current density is associated with stronger heating risk.
For JEE, keep the chain visible: microscopic carriers give drift speed, drift
speed gives current density, and conductivity links current density to
electric
field.
The equations are connected, not a collection of unrelated formulas.
Now connect the field picture to a measurable circuit relation.
For an ohmic conductor at fixed temperature and fixed physical conditions,
potential difference is proportional to current.
We write V equals I R.
Resistance measures how strongly the element opposes charge flow in that
condition.
The phrase fixed conditions matters.
A metal filament heats as current rises, so its resistance changes; a diode is
even more clearly non ohmic.
On a graph, read the axes before grabbing a slope.
If vertical is V and horizontal is I, the slope is R.
If vertical is I and horizontal is V, the slope is one over R.
That small habit prevents many JEE mistakes.
Here is a short example.
A resistor has twelve volts across it and carries three amperes.
Its resistance is four ohms.
If the same resistor remains at the same temperature and we apply twenty
volts,
the current becomes five amperes.
Pause and ask: what assumption allowed that prediction?
It was not merely the label resistor; it was the ohmic, fixed condition model.
The microscopic story also makes sense.
A stronger field gives carriers more drift between collisions, so current
density rises proportionally while the material and geometry stay stable.
A graph that bends tells us the proportionality has changed.
In practice, contact resistance, heating and material behavior can matter.
In JEE questions, identify the model first, then use the graph or equation.
Never call every two terminal device ohmic just because it has a voltage and a
current.
Resistance has two layers.
Geometry matters through R equals rho L over A, while resistivity rho belongs
to the material and its physical condition.
A longer uniform wire gives carriers more length over which collisions can
impede drift.
A larger cross section offers more parallel paths, so resistance falls.
For a given metal over a modest temperature range, we often model resistivity
as rho equals rho zero times one plus alpha times T minus T zero.
Metals usually have positive alpha: heating increases resistivity.
Semiconductors can behave differently, so do not transfer the metal sign
automatically.
Try a geometry question.
A uniform wire is stretched to twice its original length, with volume
conserved.
If its radius becomes r prime, the volume relation says the new area is half
the old area.
Since resistance is proportional to L over A, the new resistance is two
divided
by one half, or four times the original.
This answer uses a hidden assumption: uniform stretching and constant
resistivity.
If the wire is heated substantially, rho may change too, and the simple factor
of four is incomplete.
Another useful distinction: resistivity has units ohm meter and does not
depend
on the sample's length or area, while resistance has units ohm and does.
A material can have low resistivity but still form a large resistance if made
into a very long, thin wire.
In a graph or numerical question, list what changed: material, temperature,
length, area or all four.
That checklist keeps geometry and material effects from getting mixed
together.
Finally, let us track what the circuit is doing with energy.
Electrical power is the rate of energy transfer, P equals V I.
For an ohmic resistor, substitute V equals I R to get P equals I squared R, or
substitute I equals V over R to get P equals V squared over R.
These forms are equivalent only when the same resistor model applies.
The safest choice depends on what the question gives and what remains fixed.
A six ohm heater carries two amperes.
Its power is I squared R, which is four times six, or twenty four watts.
In five minutes, the energy transferred is power times time: twenty four
multiplied by three hundred seconds, or seven thousand two hundred joules.
Now compare two resistors across the same ideal voltage.
Since P equals V squared over R, the smaller resistance takes the larger
power.
With the same current through them, P equals I squared R, so the larger
resistance takes the larger power.
Same symbols, different constraint, different comparison.
That is a classic JEE trap.
Power is not the same as energy: watts measure joules per second, while energy
is measured in joules.
In a real resistor, electrical energy becomes internal energy and then often
heat transferred to the surroundings.
We have now built a clean foundation: charge flow gives current, the material
and geometry give resistance, and voltage current conditions determine power.
The next classes will use these ideas in resistor networks, cells and
Kirchhoff
laws, where node by node bookkeeping becomes the main skill.
